casting-call: New-Machine Setup, End to End

Everything it takes to go from a fresh Mac to a working call-recording rig: install the tools, record a screen call as three separate audio tracks (you, the far side, and a marker track), and turn it into a transcript with your flagged moments dropped in at the right spot. Follow it top to bottom the first time.

Sections are tagged terminal when they are copy-paste commands (safe to hand to an agent) or in the app when they are clicks in OBS or Stream Deck that only a human can do. The flow the whole thing produces is in docs/pipeline-flow.html if you want the picture first.

What you end up with

OBS records your screen plus three audio tracks into one .mkv. Track 1 is your mic, Track 2 is the far side (Chrome, where Meet runs), and Track 3 is silent except for the short "mark flag" / "mark action" clips a Stream Deck button fires. After the call, one command splits the tracks, transcribes them, cleans up the junk Whisper invents on silence, and folds your markers in as [MARKER] lines. If the far side ever drops out, the captions on screen are the backup.

Part 1: The command line terminal

This whole part is safe to run start to finish. It installs the tools, pulls the repo, and regenerates the marker clips locally (the .wav files are gitignored, so they do not come down with the clone).

# Homebrew, if this machine does not have it yet
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"

# Tools: ffmpeg + whisper for audio, tesseract for the caption fallback, the apps
brew install ffmpeg whisper-cpp tesseract
brew install --cask obs elgato-stream-deck

# Python deps (Homebrew's python3; --break-system-packages is required on it)
pip3 install --break-system-packages pillow numpy pytesseract pytest

# Whisper model, ~3 GB, one time
mkdir -p ~/whisper-models
curl -o ~/whisper-models/ggml-large-v3.bin -L \
  'https://huggingface.co/ggerganov/whisper.cpp/resolve/main/ggml-large-v3.bin?download=true'

# Silero VAD model (~1 MB, one time) so Whisper only transcribes real speech and
# stops inventing looped lines on non-speech audio
curl -sL -o ~/whisper-models/ggml-silero-v5.1.2.bin \
  https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/whisper-vad/resolve/main/ggml-silero-v5.1.2.bin

# The repo
git clone https://github.com/samgutentag/casting-call.git ~/Developer/casting-call
cd ~/Developer/casting-call

# Your roster (real names stay local; this file is gitignored)
cp speakers_roster.example.json speakers_roster.json
# then edit speakers_roster.json: set "self" to your name, list the people you call

# Marker clips (regenerated here; not committed)
mkdir -p obs/marker-clips
for p in flag important action question quote; do
  say -o /tmp/_m.aiff "mark $p"
  ffmpeg -loglevel error -i /tmp/_m.aiff -ar 16000 -ac 1 -c:a pcm_s16le "obs/marker-clips/mark-$p.wav" -y
done
rm -f /tmp/_m.aiff

# Confirm the toolchain is sane
python3 -m pytest -q

If the tests pass, the software side is done. The clips now live in ~/Developer/casting-call/obs/marker-clips/, which you will point OBS at in Part 3.

If python3 offers to install "command line developer tools," let it, then rerun the last two commands. The scripts and Whisper only need what you just installed.

Part 2: OBS, recording three tracks in the app

OBS records MKV on purpose. If a recording ever crashes, an MKV is still readable where an MP4 would be corrupt. You never remux it; the pipeline reads the MKV directly.

  1. Open OBS. Skip or click through the auto-config wizard.
  2. Settings, Output. Set Output Mode to Advanced. On the Recording tab set Recording Format to Matroska Video (.mkv), and under Audio Track check 1, 2, and 3.
  3. Sources. Add these to your scene:
    1. Display Capture (or Window Capture) for the screen. This is the video.
    2. Audio Input Capture pointed at your mic (the Elgato Wave). This is you.
    3. Application Audio Capture targeting Google Chrome, not the Meet PWA. Chrome routes call audio through one process that captures reliably; the PWA often records silent.
  4. Assign tracks. Click the gear in the Audio Mixer, choose Advanced Audio Properties. For each source, use the Tracks checkboxes on the right:
    • Mic (you): Track 1 only.
    • Chrome (far side): Track 2 only.
Do not switch your Mac's audio devices to route the call. That was the old rig, and it dropped the mic to Meet mid-call. OBS only reads audio, so Meet keeps your real mic and headphones. Leave them alone.

Part 3: The marker track in the app

This is the piece that makes markers work without any syncing. Five clips, each on its own media source, all routed to Track 3, none of them ever heard by anyone live.

  1. Add five Media Source items to the scene, one per clip in obs/marker-clips/ (mark-flag.wav through mark-quote.wav). In each media source, uncheck Loop and check "Restart playback when source becomes active."
  2. In Advanced Audio Properties, for all five marker sources:
    • Tracks: 3 only (uncheck 1 and 2 so markers never touch the voice tracks).
    • Audio Monitoring: Monitor Off. This is what keeps the clip out of your headphones and, more importantly, out of anything Meet can pick up. It still records to Track 3.
Why nobody hears it: an OBS media source plays inside OBS. With Monitor Off, OBS records it to Track 3 but never sends it to an output device, and OBS never feeds audio back into your mic or Meet. So the marker is silent to you and to the caller, and still lands in the file.

Part 4: Stream Deck buttons in the app

  1. Open the Stream Deck app and install the official OBS Studio plugin from its Marketplace. In OBS, enable Tools, WebSocket Server Settings, Enable WebSocket server so Stream Deck can talk to it.
  2. Start / Stop. Drag the OBS Start Recording action onto a key, and Stop Recording onto another.
  3. Five marker keys. Use the OBS plugin's Media Source Control action (search "media" in the actions list), one per key. Set each key's Media Source to the matching source (Mark Flag, Mark Important, Mark Action, Mark Question, Mark Quote) and its action to Restart, so every press plays the clip from the top. This is the action that works; "Source Visibility" does not trigger playback, so do not use it here.
The one gotcha that will silently eat your markers: the marker sources live on Track 3, so the recording output has to actually record Track 3. Confirm Settings, Output, Recording has Audio Tracks 1, 2, and 3 checked. If Track 3 is off, the buttons fire, the clips play, and none of it ends up in the file. Sanity check a test recording with ffprobe recording.mkv and count three audio streams.

Part 5: Prove it works before a real call terminal + in the app

  1. In OBS, press Start, talk for a few seconds, press a couple of marker keys, then press Stop. Move the resulting .mkv into a folder, say ~/calls/test/.
  2. Confirm the file really has three audio tracks: 
    ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=index,codec_type -of csv ~/calls/test/*.mkv
# expect one 'video' line and three 'audio' lines
  3. Run the pipeline and read the result: 
    cd ~/Developer/casting-call
bash bin/extract_audio_stereo.sh ~/calls/test
cat ~/calls/test/transcripts/*.txt
    You should see [You] and [Caller] lines with [MARKER] lines sitting inline wherever you pressed a key.

If the markers land in the right place and nobody heard them during the test, the rig is done.

Part 6: The daily loop

  1. Start recording in OBS (or via the Stream Deck key). Tap the marker keys during the call whenever something matters.
  2. Stop. Drop the .mkv in a folder.
  3. bash bin/extract_audio_stereo.sh <folder>. That is the transcript, markers and all, ready to hand to an LLM.
  4. Optional, only when you want to watch it back: bash bin/convert_video.sh <folder> renders a playable .mp4 with you on the left channel and the caller on the right.
  5. Optional, to put real names on the far-side lines: bash bin/extract_speakers.sh <recording> --region x,y,w,h --transcript <transcript>.

Part 7: When the far side drops out

Chrome's audio capture can die mid-call and record silence from that point on. The pipeline watches for it: if Track 2 goes quiet for a sustained stretch, it prints a warning with the timestamp and points you at the recovery tool. The lines Whisper would have invented on that dead audio are stripped automatically, so the transcript does not fill up with fake "thank you" and "subtitles by" junk.

To get the lost words back, the Meet captions on screen are the source:

bash bin/stitch_captions.sh <recording> --region x,y,w,h

The one catch, learned the hard way: the caption region is fixed, so the Meet window has to stay in one place and size for the whole call. If you move or resize it, a single region will not cover the recording, and you are into recovering one layout at a time. Park the Meet window and leave it.
